docs.t: Done (2026-11-14), step 2: recovery.efi and its checks. systools/mkefi.sh makes /EFI/rudolf/recovery.efi beside rudolf.efi on every disc's and boot image's ESP, signed in the same step with SB_KEY (the workflow's secret bundle's .initrd (unpacked over the kernel's own) holding /etc/rudolf-recovery (the mark), /etc/rudolf-official-key (iso/trusted-keys.txt, exactly one key: the official one; RUDOLF_TEST_KEYS in local test builds only) and an empty initramfs for the handover; its fixed options add rudolf.recovery=1. The boot menu's "Recovery mode" entry (loader/entries/rudolf-recovery.conf) starts recovery.efi. With the mark, initramfs/init starts only system/r, after official_check: its manifest's signature with the official key alone (rudolf-verity check; extra-keys never read, and said when one is there), the list being a system list naming each of the five files once, and every file's size and SHA-256; then kexec of system/r's kernel (rudolf.slot=r rudolf.official=1, Secure Boot's lockdown passed on). Anything wrong: a refusal naming the file and the reason, and nothing else started in its place (a rescue stick is the way on). With no system/r on the drive at all (a disc or stick never installed), the drive's own system, its layers checked with the official key alone, even with Secure Boot off. Without the mark (older boot files, rudolf.efi) nothing changed. Found

docs.t: Who may change it: only rudolf-update, with an official release. A custom build's updater is told by the official rules (and its own copy of them) to leave system/r and recovery.efi alone; the official build checks both at each start and repairs them from the official release if they were changed.

docs.t: The honest limit: an administrator, or a custom build running as root, can always overwrite their own disk, including these files. Secure Boot then refuses a recovery file not signed by an enrolled key, so the entry either starts the real official recovery or does not start at all; it cannot start a fake one unless the developer's own key signed it. The last way back is the same as on 2026-11-10: a rescue stick made from an official release (Make a stick, or the official boot image from GitHub, 1.5.7), which starts the official recovery from USB.

docs.t: In Settings › Updates (Developer mode › Turn off) and in Recovery mode's first screen: 1. removes the extra key and the developer's update address, and sets the official address; 2. starts from system/r (or downloads the newest official release, checked with the official key) into the spare slot, and makes it the one that starts; the slot the custom build was in is cleared; 3. restores the official rudolf.efi from that release; 4. asks: keep accounts, files and apps (a return), or erase everything (a factory reset, as Install here does, without a disc); 5. after the next start, Settings › About says Official Rudolf OS again, and the self-test checks it.

docs.t: Done (2026-11-13): rudolf-update return-official keep|erase (Developer mode off; slot r, or the newest official release downloaded, into the spare slot, tried at the next start; once it started, boot-ok clears every slot that is not official; erase: the factory reset at that start, the system slots kept); rudolfd sys/return (a job); Settings › Update and recovery's button and Recovery mode's notice. Not yet: restoring the official rudolf.efi (8.4's ESP work), and Library apps from outside developers checked against their certificates (8.2's certificates). If the official start fails, the start-up falls back to the previous slot as every update does, and Recovery mode is still there.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 9: game mode frees memory for the game (added on 2026-11-11)
docs.t: Found on the Vivobook (1.5.8 beta 2026111108, Standard desktop): Friday Night Funkin' on Newgrounds holds about 1.7 GB. While a song played, 400 MB of the 3.4 GB stayed free, the swap gave memory back in the first seconds of the song, and the game stuttered, with the processor at about 21% overall (3.5-3.9 GHz, 67-71 °C) and the graphics chip mostly idle: memory is what is short, not speed. Before 1.5.8 the memory guard ended the game outright (PR #203).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 9: game mode frees memory for the game (added on 2026-11-11) › 9.1 When it applies
docs.t: Game mode (game51.js, 1.5.1) already starts when a page is full screen or has the pointer captured; it also starts for a Steam game's window or a Flatpak game in front (Games category), and by hand from the taskbar (🎮). Settings › Games › Game mode › "Free memory for the game" (on by default), each part below with its own switch. It ends when the game leaves full screen or loses the front; what was paused comes back then, or when used.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 9: game mode frees memory for the game (added on 2026-11-11) › 9.2 What it does
docs.t: 1. Oracle's other tabs sleep: tabs not in front, not playing sound, not in a call (Part 7) and not loading a form the person typed into are unloaded (the shell and rudolf-webkit close their page and keep the address, title, icon and scroll position); selecting one loads it again. On Standard and on Lite. The desktop says how many slept. 2. The desktop gets smaller: animated wallpapers, the desktop's widgets and hidden windows' timers pause; the desktop's own caches (thumbnails, the App Store's catalog) are dropped. 3. Background work waits: update and Library downloads, the Linux apps' and Debian's background updates, the file index, Blitzen's model (if loaded, about 1-2 GB: unloaded, loaded again when Blitzen is opened).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 9: game mode frees memory for the game (added on 2026-11-11) › 9.2 What it does
docs.t: 4. Apps in the tray: apps with no window open (Discord, chat apps) are offered to be quit in one notification ("Free 600 MB for the game? Quit Discord, …"), never quit without asking; the memory guard still steps in when memory really runs out (its rules, PR #203). 5. The game comes first: while game mode is on, the memory guard ends background tabs and pages before the game's, the game's processes get a lower oom_score_adj than other pages', and the kernel is asked to move other programs' memory to the swap first (memory.reclaim on the desktop's and background apps' cgroups at the start, while the game loads), so the game's own loading does not wait on the swap.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 9: game mode frees memory for the game (added on 2026-11-11) › 9.2a Compressed memory as large as the memory (added on 2026-11-12)
docs.t: Found on the Vivobook (final 1.5.8 beta 2026111218): FNF reached 1.9 GB when a song ended and the game went back to song selection; with 143 MB available and the compressed swap (zram) all but full (287 of 1,707 MB free), the memory guard ended the game. zram compressed about 4 to 1 there, so the swap filled long before the memory was used up. The Vivobook's Settings › System health › Memory is on "small" (half the memory, 1.7 GB); the default since 1.5.7, "auto", is as large as the memory (3.4 GB here, at most 8 GB).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 9: game mode frees memory for the game (added on 2026-11-11) › 9.2a Compressed memory as large as the memory (added on 2026-11-12)
docs.t: Measure first, on the Vivobook: zram on auto, the same FNF test (a whole week, back to song selection each time): the guard's events, the swap used and the stalls (PSI), and frame times, against "small". Then, if auto keeps the game alive without long stalls: when the guard ends a page or an app and zram is on "small", its notification offers to switch to auto (applies at the next restart); game mode (9.1) says the same once. If auto stalls more than it helps, the guard's thresholds are tuned with it instead (its "memory is low" point and the stall it waits for).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 9: game mode frees memory for the game (added on 2026-11-11) › 9.2a Compressed memory as large as the memory (added on 2026-11-12)
docs.t: Tests: host, the size zram is given for auto and small on 2, 3.4, 4 and 16 GB (the memory script); browser, the offer in the notification and the switch. Measured on 2026-11-12 (beta 2026111222, zram on auto, 3.4 GB): FNF was still ended, at 1,929 MiB: 130 MiB available with 2.4 GB of zram free and real stalls (8%). The game took memory faster than the kernel moved idle memory into zram. Chosen: swappiness 180 (was 100), so it moves sooner; the warning (9.2b) no longer waits for the swap to fill. Measured again with FNF on the next beta.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 9: game mode frees memory for the game (added on 2026-11-11) › 9.2a Compressed memory as large as the memory (added on 2026-11-12)
docs.t: The file cache cleared when game mode starts (2026-11-12, asked for): rudolfd memory/dropcache (clean cached files only, drop_caches 1, once every 10 s at most), called once per game by game mode and by Task Manager › Performance › Clear cache. Linux gives the cache back by itself, but more slowly than a game can ask.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 9: game mode frees memory for the game (added on 2026-11-11) › 9.2b The memory guard warns before it ends the game (added on 2026-11-12)
docs.t: On 2026-11-12 the guard ended FNF (about 2 GB) twice without a word before it: the screen left full screen and said so afterwards (1.5.8). When memory is low but not yet critical and the largest page is the one in front (above all full screen), the guard first asks the desktop to warn: a small notice over the full-screen page ("Memory is almost full: close other tabs or apps to keep the game running", with the largest of them and a button for each), for at least 10 seconds or until memory is critical, whichever comes first. A background page is still ended first, as now; the warning is only for the page in front. Tests: host, the guard's new "low, warned" step and its timings; browser, the notice over a full-screen page and its buttons.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 10: a lighter desktop page (added on 2026-11-12)
docs.t: the System monitor (all memory minus what Linux calls available), of which the desktop's own processes about 500 to 550 MB, the kernel about 130 MB, about 200 to 250 MB that belongs to no process (steady at idle, after a video and after a game: not a graphics pool that fills with use, so capping TTM's page_pool_size would gain little here), and shared memory and file cache. Lite (1.5.7's check): the page's own process 389 MB of about 520 MB. Most of the page's share is the page itself: 4.8 MB of code in 95 modules, all loaded and compiled at sign-in, with every dynamic background (light and dark, about 1.5 MB as text), fonts and the CHANGELOG embedded. Slimming it helps both engines.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 10: a lighter desktop page (added on 2026-11-12)
docs.t: What the 200 to 250 MB is was read on 2026-11-12 with one start without lockdown (docs/plan-memdebug.md): 40 to 65 MB is graphics (the driver's page pool, 21 to 46 MB and growing with use, and the system memory the graphics card uses); 140 to 180 MB is taken by the kernel or a driver outside every counter, to be named by a test kernel with allocation profiling. From it: The graphics pool capped (ttm page_pool_size 16384 pages = 64 MB, in /etc/modules/ttm and by the memory script; done in 1.5.9): its limit is now 1.7 GB, so it can creep up over a long session. Measured: the frame rate of a video and of FNF before and after.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 10: a lighter desktop page (added on 2026-11-12)
docs.t: What the test kernel names, each with its own fix. Task Manager says where the memory goes (asked for on 2026-11-12, done): rudolfd's memory/breakdown and Performance › "Where the memory goes": programs and web pages, the file cache, the kernel, graphics, the SSD's host memory buffer (noted by the memory script from the start-up messages), compressed memory, and "Other drivers and kernel" for what cannot be read with lockdown on (the graphics pool, network buffers, early start-up), saying so.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 10: a lighter desktop page (added on 2026-11-12) › 10.1 What moves out of the start-up page
docs.t: Pictures and fonts first: the dynamic backgrounds, their thumbnails and the sky masks (DYN), and the extra fonts, become files beside the page; only the background in use is loaded and decoded, the thumbnails when Display Properties opens, a font when chosen. Self-contained apps: WordPro, the spreadsheet and presentations, the games, Emu, BlockLua, Blitzen's packs, the Library apps' pages, Help and What's new: each its own file, loaded when first opened. What stays: the core (windows, taskbar, Settings' frame, Oracle and its tabs, the shell's messages) and every module that wraps a shared function (applySet, dispPanelS, themeApply, lxRun and the like: aurora58, statue58, accent56, lock58 among them), since the order they wrap in matters.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 10: a lighter desktop page (added on 2026-11-12) › 10.2 Without causing issues
docs.t: A stub per app: the name stays defined from the start; the first call loads the file, then runs the call (a .docx opened from File Explorer, a game from the Library, a Help link). A file that cannot load says so, with Try again, never a silent failure. Versioned file names (wordpro-1.5.9-ab12.js): a desktop open across an update never mixes versions; the old files stay until the next start. Everywhere the page runs: rudolfd serves the files for both engines (127.0.0.1:8080, and rudolf-webkit's own loading); the browser build on GitHub Pages ships them beside index.html, and the phone web app's offline cache (7.5) stores them.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 10: a lighter desktop page (added on 2026-11-12) › 10.2 Without causing issues
docs.t: The tools learn it: build19.py writes the files and their list; deadcheck reads them all; the self-test checks every listed file is present; each app's browser tests load it through its stub. Chromium cannot unload code: the saving is in apps not opened in a session; the memory their documents and pictures use is still given back when they close (checked: no references kept after a window closes).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 10: a lighter desktop page (added on 2026-11-12) › 10.3 Then, measured
docs.t: The engines' own limits: Lite's JavaScript heap and, for the desktop page only, the JIT off as an option measured for speed; Standard's renderer limit and the desktop page's heap limit (site isolation stays on for websites). The ~200 MB that belongs to no process: what it is (kernel, graphics driver; debugfs is locked down with Secure Boot, so through the driver's sysfs counters and /proc), and whether any of it can be given back. WPE WebKit as a later Lite engine (no GTK layer), measured against WebKitGTK, once the page is slim.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 10: a lighter desktop page (added on 2026-11-12) › 10.4 Targets and tests
docs.t: Targets at the sign-in screen, nothing open: Lite about 300 to 350 MB for the desktop's processes (0.55 to 0.65 GB on the System monitor), Standard about 0.8 to 0.9 GB on the System monitor; start-up no slower. Tests: browser tests that each deferred app opens through its stub on both engines, that an update between loads keeps versions apart, and that a missing file is reported; on the Vivobook, memory at idle and after opening and closing each large app, Standard and Lite, before promotion.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 11: fixes and safeguards (added on 2026-11-12) › 11.5 The Wi-Fi's radios, and Blitzen's Wi-Fi diagnosis (asked for on 2026-11-13, done)
docs.t: On 2026111302 the Vivobook left the router's 5 GHz radio for its 2.4 GHz one, which never answers it, and was off for 45 s. Now: a radio that did not answer is left out for a day (wifi-event, the kernel's own message counted); Settings › Network › Wi-Fi › "Radios of this network" lists each radio (band, channel, signal, state) with a Use switch (wifi.sh radios / radio; turned off by hand it stays off); "Why does the Wi-Fi drop?" (and a Wi-Fi problem asked in Blitzen's chat) gives Blitzen the Wi-Fi's log, the kernel's Wi-Fi messages and the radios (ai/facts), with a Wi-Fi pack that says how to read them and which settings exist. To check on the Vivobook: Blitzen's real answer.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 11: fixes and safeguards (added on 2026-11-12) › 11.5 The Wi-Fi's radios, and Blitzen's Wi-Fi diagnosis (asked for on 2026-11-13, done)
docs.t: This computer's Wi-Fi radios (asked for on 2026-11-13): a drop-down menu between "Radios of this network" and "Why does the Wi-Fi drop?", listing the computer's own radios (its adapter's bands, 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz) with a check by each one that is on and a blank space by one that is off. Only an administrator changes it, typing their password every time. Kept by the adapter's MAC (/persist/etc/wifi-bands-off), applied as wpa_supplicant's freq_list at every start and join (wifi.sh bands / band); nothing automatic writes it, a router's radio on a band that is off cannot be turned on in "Radios of this network", and Blitzen never recommends against it. One radio always stays on.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 11: fixes and safeguards (added on 2026-11-12) › 11.1 Chromium from one known source, never changed without being chosen
docs.t: On 2026-11-12 the snap store could not be reached for four builds in a row, and each time the build fell back to Playwright's Chromium without being asked. Newer Playwright brings Google's Chrome for Testing (158.0.8127.18), which is what 1.5.8 shipped: a Google Chrome build made for automated tests, not for everyday browsing, under Google's own terms rather than Chromium's open-source licence. Rudolf OS ships open-source Chromium. One source: Ubuntu's chromium snap (open-source Chromium, built for Ubuntu like the base layer). Debian's package is no alternative: it is built for Debian's newer C library and does not run on the Ubuntu base. The download is made sturdier: the store's two addresses (api.snapcraft.io and its CDN), longer retries.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 11: fixes and safeguards (added on 2026-11-12) › 11.1 Chromium from one known source, never changed without being chosen
docs.t: No silent fallback: when the snap cannot be fetched, the release keeps the previous release's chromium.sfs (as it already does when the start test fails) and says so in its notes and as a warning. Playwright stays only for local test builds and by explicit choice (CHROMIUM_FROM=playwright). Checked before it is used: chrome --version must say "Chromium" (not "Google Chrome"), and the version must not be lower than the release's: Chromium does not open a profile written by a newer version, so 1.5.8's Chrome for Testing 158 stays until the snap has 158 or newer. The release notes say when the Chromium was kept and why. Tests: host, chromium_fetch.sh against recorded store answers (a timeout, Chrome branding, a lower version).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 11: fixes and safeguards (added on 2026-11-12) › 11.2 Browser security updates
docs.t: Chromium has security fixes every few weeks, and they reach Rudolf OS only with a release. A scheduled workflow, once a day, compares the snap's stable Chromium with the stable release's and, when it is newer, opens (or updates) one GitHub issue: "Chromium X is available (security fixes): the stable release has Y". A beta with it is then one dispatch; promotion stays the person's choice. (1.5.9 15.6's security check replaces it, with the kernel too.)

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 11: fixes and safeguards (added on 2026-11-12) › 11.3 A clear message when a system layer does not match its release
docs.t: When a layer differs from the signed release list, rudolf-verity reports the device-mapper's error ("table: Argument list too long") instead of saying what is wrong. It compares the layer's size with the list's blocks before loading the table and says "modules.sfs does not match the release list (size)"; Task Manager and the start-up message show that. Test: host, a layer of another size.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 11: fixes and safeguards (added on 2026-11-12) › 11.4 New features keep their logic in the system services
docs.t: So that the desktop that draws them can change (the native desktop decision after 1.6.0), what 1.5.9 adds (the modem service, Share this connection, calls, game mode, developer mode) keeps its logic and state in rudolfd and the services, with the desktop only showing state and sending choices through rudolfd's API. Each part's API is written down in docs/api.md with its first use.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 12: the native desktop engine, a prototype (added on 2026-11-13) › 12.1 What it is
docs.t: rudolf-native (C and GTK 3, which the system layer already has for Lite's WebKitGTK: no new libraries) draws: - the wallpaper: a drawn background (its light or dark picture), a picture of your own, or the colours; - the taskbar: the start menu, the pinned apps, the open windows, the clock, and the tray (network, sound, battery, notifications' count) from rudolfd's API; - every window's frame, as the window manager: the title bar (Part's title bar styles and colours: twstyle, twacm), minimise, maximise, close, moving and resizing, focus; - the sign-in and lock screens, with rudolfd checking the password (the accounts' hashes never reach rudolf-native).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 12: the native desktop engine, a prototype (added on 2026-11-13) › 12.1 What it is
docs.t: The apps stay web pages: an app opens in a WebKit window of its own showing the desktop page in one-app mode (index.html#app=notepad: the page starts that app alone, filling its window, without taskbar, icons or wallpaper). All app windows share one WebKit web process, so the page's code is loaded once, not once per window. Linux apps and Oracle's tabs (Chromium) are framed windows like any other.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 12: the native desktop engine, a prototype (added on 2026-11-13) › 12.2 Decisions (2026-11-13)
docs.t: X11, not Wayland, for the prototype: everything around the desktop is X11 today (rudolf-display's input and its Wayland compositor would change all of them at once and the measurement would no longer compare engines alone. Wayland becomes part of the 2.0 decision. State stays in rudolfd (11.4): what the native shell needs that only the web page knows today (the desktop's settings, the pinned apps, the accounts) is read through rudolfd's API, from the copy of the page's storage it already keeps (lsync, /home/rudolf/.rudolf-ls.json); rudolf-native never parses the page's storage itself. Not in the prototype: desktop icons' editing, widgets, Phone screen, Blitzen's panel, drag and drop between windows, multiple workspaces. They come with 2.0 if it goes ahead.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 12: the native desktop engine, a prototype (added on 2026-11-13) › 12.3 Steps
docs.t: 1. The page's one-app mode (#app=NAME): one app, filling the window; closing it closes the page; on both engines. 2. rudolfd: GET desktop/settings (background, title bars, taskbar position, pins, clock, accent) and desktop/apps (the start menu's list, written by the page) from the lsync copy; POST login (checks a password, opens the account's encrypted folder as the page's sign-in does). 3. rudolf-native: wallpaper, taskbar, start menu, clock, tray. 4. rudolf-native: the window manager (frames, focus, minimise, maximise, close, move, resize) and the taskbar's list. 5. The session: Native (test) in Settings, its trial and give-up as Lite's.

docs.t: Asked for: Oracle on the native desktop runs on Chromium, so that it works exactly as on Standard (docs/plan-1.6.0.md Part 12, "The rule"). Found on 2026-11-14: on Native, Oracle opens as any app does, its page in a WebKit one-app window, and nothing there gives it real tabs (no rudolfShell: only rudolf-native's rudolfNative message handler), so its websites fall back to frames, or to a separate Chromium window for sign-in sites. Many sites refuse frames; sign-ins are not kept as on Standard; private tabs are not private (Part 14); games run in a frame of the WebKit page. 12.1's "Oracle's tabs (Chromium) are framed windows like any other" assumed a step that was never written: this one.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 12: the native desktop engine, a prototype (added on 2026-11-13) › 12.3c Step 8: Oracle on Native runs on Chromium, as on Standard (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: Why Chromium and not something else (decided 2026-11-14): Blink (drawing pages) and V8 (JavaScript) are parts of Chromium and cannot be used alone; whatever embeds them (CEF, Qt WebEngine, Electron) ships a Chromium of its own, a second copy (about 100 MB more) with a different build. WebKitGTK tabs, as Lite has, would be lighter but are Safari's engine: sites and games behave differently. Rudolf's own Chromium with its tab shell is the same program as Standard's: the same Blink and V8, the same partitions (an account's sign-ins are the same on both engines), private tabs in memory, nothing more to download. How:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 12: the native desktop engine, a prototype (added on 2026-11-13) › 12.3c Step 8: Oracle on Native runs on Chromium, as on Standard (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: 1. Oracle's window on Native is Chromium with the shell (iso/shell, the Isolated Web App Standard starts), not a WebKit one-app window: when Oracle is opened (the start menu, a pin, a desktop icon, a link from another app, a file of a web type, a page's "open in Oracle"), rudolf-native starts /opt/chromium/chrome --class=RudolfOracle --user-data-dir=PROFILE --app=isolated-app://SHELLID/#app=browser&url=… with Standard's flags (the session's: GPU flags, features turned off, autoplay, the fake media UI for calls, the password store), as the account's Linux user. The shell passes its own #… on to the desktop frame (DESK_URL + location.hash), so the page inside starts Oracle alone in one-app mode (oneapp59.js), now with the shell's real tabs (rtOn() true): Standard's code path, unchanged.

The windows are framed by rudolf-native's window manager like the others (the page's title bars, the taskbar's button with Oracle's icon and title; RudolfOracle grouped as Oracle, not as a Linux app).

Chromium's windows (WM_CLASS RudolfOracle) are framed as Oracle: its picture and name in the title bar and the taskbar, the title the page's (Chromium's "Rudolf OS - TITLE" without the shell's name), the pin bringing it to the front, Open a new window and Close all windows in the pin's menu as for the other apps. An Isolated Web App's window always has Chromium's own title bar and edges (measured: neither the "use the system's title bar" setting nor display_override "borderless" with the window-management permission removes them, Chromium 153), so the window manager puts the window in a clip window inside the frame, its own bar (28 px) and edges (4 px) cut away (RUDOLF_ORACLE_INSET to change them); full screen, Chromium draws none. docs.t: POST desktop/login (body {"n":NAME,"p":PASSWORD}): finds the account (bd95user), checks the password as the page does (p2$salt$hash: PBKDF2-SHA-256, 210 000 rounds), derives the password's key with the account's salt (ks), unwraps its file key (fk, AES-GCM), and for an account whose files are on the disk opens its encrypted folder with the key the page makes (HKDF-SHA-512 of the file key, "rudolf-os home folder", the account's id) and the session's binds, as home/unlock?session=1. The session is kept root-only in /run/rudolf/native-session (id, name, role, the two keys): each rudolfd connection is its own process, so state lives in files. Five wrong passwords: 15 s of "wait", as the page. Refused, with a reason the screen shows: an account with a security key, a password hash from before 1.4 (sign in once with Standard), no such account. The guest: no password, no keys. A failed sign-in goes in the health log as the page's do.

Raw values as the page keeps them; the shell computes the colours (acVariant, acInk and the shades, ported to C).

GET desktop/wallpaper?acct=ID, POST desktop/wallpaper?acct=ID: a picture of your own. It lives in the page's IndexedDB, so the page also gives rudolfd a copy (the JPEG it already shrinks to the screen) whenever it loads or changes one; kept beside the account's settings in /home/rudolf/.rudolf-wallpaper/ID.jpg. docs/api.md describes these (11.4).

docs.t: Step 3: rudolf-native's wallpaper, taskbar, start menu, clock and tray. One GTK 3 process, run as the desktop user, started by the session (step 5): rudolf-native --size=WxH [--draw=gpu|mixed|soft] [--base=http://127.0.0.1:8080]. It reads the token as the page gets it (rudolfd's page, GET /: nothing new is exposed), then talks to rudolfd over HTTP on 127.0.0.1 (a small blocking client; the sign-in in a worker thread, its reply back to GTK's loop with g_idle_add). JSON is read by a small reader of its own (found in step 3: a JavaScriptCore context made in the shell's own process stopped WebKit's views from drawing).

Choosing an app opens its window (step 4); in step 3 a pinned app or a menu item opens it as a plain WebKit window. The clock: the time (12- or 24-hour, h24), the date (df), in the settings' time zone (tz) with the clock's offset (doff); updated each minute. Clicking it opens the Clock app. The tray: network (net), sound (volume), battery (power/status), the notifications' count (how many the page keeps in bd95notif:ID, given by desktop/settings); each opens its Settings page in one-app mode (#app=settings); polled every 10 s.

Once the sign-in screen is drawn the shell sends heartbeat every 10 s, as the page does (the session's trial and watchdog need it). Step 4: the window manager. rudolf-native becomes the X window manager (SubstructureRedirect on the root, through a GDK event filter, so one GTK process does both).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 12: the native desktop engine, a prototype (added on 2026-11-13) › 12.5 How it is built (the implementation design, 2026-11-14)
docs.t: Every top-level window that is not override-redirect (Linux apps, Chromium's window for websites and Oracle's real tabs, Wine) is put in a frame: an X window of ours with the title bar drawn by the same cairo code as the app windows' (the title bar styles: twstyle, twacm, the active window coloured, the others grey), minimise, maximise and close (WM_DELETE_WINDOW, else XKillClient). Moving (dragging the title bar), resizing (the 6 px edges and corners), double-click to maximise, focus on click (WM_TAKE_FOCUS and XSetInputFocus, as rudolf-display does), raising, WM_STATE, _NET_CLIENT_LIST and _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW. Dialogs (WM_TRANSIENT_FOR) are centred over their window. A window asking for full screen (_NET_WM_STATE_FULLSCREEN, games) covers the whole screen, taskbar too, without its frame.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 12: the native desktop engine, a prototype (added on 2026-11-13) › 12.5 How it is built (the implementation design, 2026-11-14)
docs.t: App windows: a pinned app or a menu item opens a GTK window of our own with a WebKitWebView showing http://127.0.0.1:8080/#app=NAME, framed like the rest. The first app window starts the web process; every other one is opened by an open app window (the page's own window.open, kept as webNativeOpen), which WebKit keeps in that process, so they share one WebKit web process (found in step 3: a view merely made related-view to another, or to a hidden one, got a process of its own or drew nothing, WebKitGTK 2.52), and one web context (the page's storage, ~/.rudolf-native, as ~/.rudolf-webkit is Lite's). All app windows have one user content manager (WebKit gives a window opened by another its opener's anyway), so each page says which window it is (#app=NAME&w=N, in each rudolfNative message). The frame's title follows the page's title; ✕ calls window.__oneAppClose() (the app may ask to save), a second ✕ after 5 s closes it anyway; the page's close closes the window. A rudolfNative message open opens another app's window. A web process that ends is reported in each window with Reload.

docs.t: The taskbar's list: the open windows (ours and the others), the active one highlighted; a click focuses, or minimises the active one; a pinned app with a window open focuses it rather than opening another. rudolf-display keeps feeding input and copying the screen (software display) but stops managing windows while /run/rudolf/wm-native exists (the session makes it before starting rudolf-native and removes it after: rudolf-native runs as the desktop user, who cannot write /run/rudolf).

docs.t: Step 5: the session. Settings › System health › Desktop engine gets Native (test); rudolfd's desktop/engine takes engine=native (when /usr/bin/rudolf-native is there), kept in /persist/etc/rudolf-desktop-engine as Lite's. The session's native_usable (the choice is native, not Recovery mode, not given up this start, the binary is there) comes before Lite's check; ENGINE=native starts rudolf-native as the desktop user in the desktop's memory group. Its safeguards are Lite's, shared: the trial mark (.trying) made when it starts and removed at its first heartbeat; a start that did not reach the sign-in screen gives it up at the next start; no heartbeat in 90 s, or closing three times in a row as it starts, gives it up now. Given up means Standard (Chromium) from then on, said in System health ("the Native desktop did not start (…), so the standard engine is used from now on"), as Lite. The watchdog's other rules stay. The release build (ci_release.sh, mkrootfs.sh, arm64_base.sh) builds rudolf-native and the webkit-check workflow builds it and runs native59_t.sh.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: Asked for after a review of how Rudolf OS stands against malware aimed at its owner (2026-11-14). Below the desktop it is strong: Secure Boot with Rudolf's own keys and a signed kernel image, read-only signed system layers, signed updates and Library packages, the a/b slots and recovery, Chromium's sandbox for websites, sandboxed Library web apps and downloads, the firewall, encrypted home folders. Above it, the review found five gaps; a directed attack would most likely get a program run (a game, an .exe, a Linux app) and go through gap 1. In this order:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: Found: rudolfd serves the desktop page, with its per-boot API token and the page's stored data (rudolf-ls), to any program that connects to 127.0.0.1:8080 (serve_index has no check). A Linux app, a Wine program or a Flatpak with network access, all running as uid 1000 like the desktop, can read the token and then drive the API, which runs as root (disks, updates, factory reset, accounts).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: Who is connecting: for each connection to 8080 (and every other loopback listener of rudolfd: 8099 and the rest, listed in 15.5), rudolfd finds the socket's process: the peer's port in /proc/net/tcp (and tcp6) gives the socket's inode and uid; the inode is looked for only among the processes of the desktop's cgroup (cgroup.procs: Chromium's, rudolf-webkit's or rudolf-native's processes, and the Chromium of Oracle on Native, Part 12 step 8). Found there: the desktop. Else: not the desktop. Done once per connection (keep-alive keeps the answer).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: What a program that is not the desktop gets: not the page (403, "This page belongs to Rudolf OS's desktop"), no /api/ (403 even with the right token), no rudolf-ls. What stays open to everyone, as now: /lib/ and /pkg/ (shared libraries with CORS for Oracle's sandboxed pages), /dlf/ (downloads, served sandboxed), the Library's web apps (sandboxed, no origin). The other programs must not be in the desktop's cgroup: every program rudolfd or the page starts (Linux apps, Flatpak, Wine, Debian, emulators, the Chromium window for websites on Lite) goes into an apps cgroup of its own, never inheriting the desktop's; checked by a test that starts each kind and reads its cgroup.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: Once each account is its own Linux user (15.3): the desktop's uid (rudolf, 1000) is required as well, from the same /proc/net/tcp line: a second check that costs nothing. Tests: host tests of rudolfd: the page and the API from a process in the desktop's cgroup (allowed), from one outside it with the right token (refused), the token never in a refused answer; QEMU: from a Flatpak app, a Wine program and a Debian terminal, curl 127.0.0.1:8080/ and an API call with a token read some other way, both refused; the desktop on each engine unaffected (Standard, Lite, Native, Oracle on Native).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.1 Only the desktop gets the page and its token (first: the most serious gap)
docs.t: Done (2026-11-14, iso/sys/rudolfd-peer.inc): "/", "/index.html" and every /api/ request are answered only for root and for processes of the desktop's memory group (the peer's socket found in /proc/net/tcp, its inode among the group's processes' descriptors; the last one that answered tried first, RUN/peer-hint). Others get 403 ("only Rudolf OS's desktop may use this"), said in System health under Security (with the Linux user, once a minute at most). A missing or empty desktop group is not enforced (so the desktop is never shut out of its own page), said once in System health and failed by the self-test's new desktop-guard line. Also: Yama in the kernel (SECURITY_YAMA, ptrace_scope 1), so a program cannot read the browser's memory for the token by ptrace either; the self-test's ptrace line checks it. Programs rudolfd starts are already its children, outside the desktop's group; rudolf-native and rudolf-webkit start none of their own. Test: qt/host/peer59_t.sh (17). Still to do from this step: the QEMU check from a Flatpak app, a Wine program and a Debian terminal (with the next beta).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: Found: the built-in apps all run in the desktop's one page (one origin), so a scripting bug in how one app shows a file (a document, an SVG, an HTML or Markdown file, an e-book) would reach every app's data and the token.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: Every place a file's contents become HTML (innerHTML, srcdoc, document.write of file-derived text, inline SVG, data: and blob: documents) is listed by a check (iso/systools/htmlsinks.py, run before each PR like deadcheck) and either escapes the text or shows it in a frame with sandbox and no allow-same-origin (no origin: no storage, no token, no parent), its scripts off unless the app needs them (the PDF viewer's PDF.js, already a sandboxed page). WordLite's and WordPro's .docx, the e-book reader, Markdown and HTML previews, SVG in the picture viewer (as , never inline), File Explorer's previews, Notepad's HTML view, the Help pages from packages.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: The page's own Content-Security-Policy, sent by rudolfd: connect-src limited to rudolfd and the services the desktop names (Open-Meteo, the Library, the update server, the time servers' HTTPS fallback), object-src none, base-uri none, frame-ancestors the shell only; so injected code could not send anything out even if it ran. Inline scripts stay allowed for now (the page is built that way); moving them to hashes is 1.6.0's. Tests: a set of hostile files (scripts in every place each format allows them) opened in each app: nothing runs in the desktop's origin (a canary in the page is never read); the CSP blocks a fetch to an outside address. Done (2026-11-14):

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: Found by the hostile-files test (qt/shell2/hostile59_t.js: 19 hostile files, each opened in every app that opens it and by default, 64 openings, plus File Explorer, Open with, Properties, Recent and notifications): the apps already escape names and contents, and Oracle shows HTML and SVG files in frames with sandbox="allow-scripts" only (no origin). One gap: WordPro's clean() was a set of patterns. It kept javascript: links, and a slash in place of a space () or an SVG got script past it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: desktop/sanitize59.js, safeHtml(): the browser's own parser (DOMParser, inert), removes what runs or loads, every on* attribute, srcdoc and formaction, and links and sources other than relative, #, http(s), mailto, tel, blob and data: pictures (not SVG); checked again until it settles, against mutation tricks. WordPro's clean() (opening, pasting) uses it. Test: qt/shell2/sanitize59_t.js (29 ways past a cleaner and 7 kinds of script link, what documents need kept, WordPro itself). iso/systools/htmlsinks.py, run by deadcheck.py: the places that make HTML from data, counted per file against htmlsinks.json (518 in 80 files on 2026-11-14: today's number, the hostile-files test is what checks them); a new one fails the check until it is reviewed and the list updated.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.2 A file opened in an app cannot reach the rest of the desktop
docs.t: The page's policy (rudolfd): Content-Security-Policy: object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'. connect-src is not limited: Oracle's downloads and the apps' imports fetch from any https address, so a list would stop only plain http. Inline scripts stay allowed (1.6.0). Still to do: the same test on the Vivobook's beta.

docs.t: 1.6.0 Part 10, as written there, done in 1.5.9: each account's Linux apps, Wine and Debian run as the account's own user (uid 1001 and up), so one account's programs cannot read another's files, and none is the desktop's user (15.1's second check). 1.6.0 Part 11 (elogind and polkit) stays in 1.6.0. Done, first step (2026-11-14), iso/sys/rudolfd-users.inc:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: Users: each account of the page's list (bd95user, read from the lsync copy after every lsync and at start; not the guest) gets acctUID, uid and gid 1001 and up, with no password, in audio, video, input and group 1000 (the devices' group: cameras, controllers, hidraw, the ADB phone, which mdev gives to group 1000). An account that goes loses its user (its programs stopped); the uids are kept in /persist/etc/rudolf/account-users ("ID UID [moved]", "-ID UID" for a removed one, never given again) and written into /etc (in RAM) at every start.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: Files: the account's folder (/persist/accounts/ID, encrypted with its key) and what is made in it belong to its user, 0700: no other account's user, and not the desktop's, can go in (rudolfd serves the desktop page as root). The move of existing computers: at the first start each account's folder's files owned by the desktop's user become its user's (lchown only, nothing copied), logged ("… belong to its own Linux user now: N moved"); a file that cannot be moved leaves the account to be tried again at the next start, said in the health log (Accounts) and in System health (the new "Accounts' Linux users" line, from GET accounts/users).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 15: security against a directed attack (added on 2026-11-14) › 15.3 Each account is its own Linux user (moved here from 1.6.0 Part 10)
docs.t: The session: at sign-in with the files on the disk (home_bind) the account's folder is also its user's home (/home/acctUID, a bind), /run/user/UID is its own, its session D-Bus and rudolf-portal start as it, and /run/rudolf/acct-session.env has its environment. Linux apps (rudolf-apps launch) and Flatpak apps (native run) start as the account's user with it; nobody signed in (or an account without its files on the disk, or the guest): as the desktop's user, as before. Sound: the desktop's PulseAudio offers a second socket, /run/rudolf/pulse/native, in a folder for the audio group only (in the list of listeners). Signing out (home_unbind) stops every program of the user (TERM, then KILL), its home and runtime folder go; rudolfd started again in the session keeps them.

docs.t: Debian and Wine as the account's user: while an account is signed in with its files on the disk, rudolf-debian maps Debian's "rudolf" (1000 inside) onto the account's user (acctUID) instead of the desktop's; its group stays 1000 (the devices' group, which the accounts' users are in). Decided against making a second uid in Debian's passwd: Debian's user, password, sudo and files stay as they are, only who it is outside changes. Its home is the account's folder (so Wine's prefix, ~/.wine, the programs Wine installs and their launchers and icons are the account's; the shell's settings are copied from /etc/skel when the folder has none); its /run/user/1000 is its own tmpfs with the account's session bus and the accounts' sound socket (/run/rudolf/pulse/native) bound in. Debian's own root cannot go into those (they are not its users'), so rudolf-debian places them from outside, as rebind does (open_tree, then move_mount in Debian's mount namespace). The map is made when Debian starts and kept beside its pid (/run/rudolf/debian/init.uid): when the account changes (rebind at sign-in and sign-out, or any command), Debian is stopped and started again for the new user on the next command. The command line's WebRTC policy reaches Chromium's own pages but not the shell's Controlled Frames (Oracle's tabs): a site in the Tor window gathered this computer's address (a host candidate). The tabs read the profile's setting, so both launchers write the fresh profile's Default/Preferences with webrtc.ip_handling_policy=disable_non_proxied_udp (and no other routes): then no UDP candidate (tested, against a normal window that does gather one). Chromium's SOCKS5 DNS works as written: every site's name goes to the proxy (SOCKS5's name form), none is looked up here, and the desktop page (127.0.0.1:8080) is not proxied.

New windows from it (browser(): Ctrl+N, a link's new window) are Tor windows; New private tab is a tab of it. It asks tor/start every 20 s and tor/stop when it closes (16.1's 90 s stop covers one that went without saying). Pressing again: its tabs back to a normal Oracle window (Native: op "untor", #app=browser&untor=1&url=…; Standard: POST torwin/back, which the desktop page takes with GET torwin/back every 2 s while a Tor window runs), and it closes.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-10: plan the first release of Rudolf OS that works with cellular networks, and stage what it needs in 1.5.8 and 1.5.9. It follows the mobile work in docs/plan-1.5.8.md (Parts 6 to 8) and docs/plan-1.5.9.md.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › What "cellular" means in 1.6.0
docs.t: Mobile data, by every common route, on x86 computers: a hotspot or phone on Wi-Fi (works today), a hotspot or phone over USB (1.5.8), a USB cellular stick, and a cellular module built into a laptop or tablet (M.2 WWAN cards: Quectel, Fibocom, Sierra Wireless, Telit). The SIM and the network handled in Rudolf OS: the SIM's PIN (and PUK), the operator's settings (APN) found by themselves, roaming on or off, signal, operator and network type in the taskbar, airplane mode. Living with a data plan: metered connections (1.5.8), data used this month and a limit, Wi-Fi preferred over cellular, and cellular as the fallback when Wi-Fi drops.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › What "cellular" means in 1.6.0
docs.t: Text messages, read and sent through the modem (carrier messages, sign-in codes), in a Messages app. ARM64: the first ARM64 release, for computers that start with UEFI (and QEMU), with the same cellular support. Not in 1.6.0: voice calls and emergency calls (a computer is not a phone, and emergency calling must be tested on each device before it is offered: 1.6.x, with the first phone), phones themselves (1.6.x, docs/plan-1.5.8.md 8.3), eSIM provisioning (downloading a carrier's eSIM profile), and 5G standalone features beyond what the modem does by itself.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Leanness
docs.t: Cellular support adds about 6 to 10 MB to the base layer (ModemManager, libqmi, libmbim, libqrtr, the operators' database, the kernel drivers as modules): measured in the release check against a 15 MB budget. ModemManager starts only when a modem is present (mdev starts it on the first modem it sees), so a computer without one runs nothing more. The Messages app is part of the desktop page (no new engine), and keeps messages in the account's folder.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 1. Modems (needs 1.5.9's ModemManager)
docs.t: ModemManager, with QMI, MBIM, QRTR and AT support, in the system layer; its D-Bus API read by rudolfd (mobile/*). FCC unlock: many laptop modules (Lenovo's and Dell's Fibocom and Quectel cards) start with their radio locked until the computer unlocks them. ModemManager's unlock scripts ship but are off; Settings offers "Turn on this laptop's cellular module" for the modules that need it, saying what it does, administrators only. Modules that Linux supports only partly (Intel's XMM7360 in some ThinkPads) are named in Settings with what is known about them, rather than failing silently.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 2. SIM and network (Settings › Mobile network)
docs.t: The SIM: present or not, locked with a PIN (asked once, by an administrator; three tries; the PUK after that, with the warning that a wrong PUK blocks the SIM for good), and the operator. The operator's settings (APN) from mobile-broadband-provider-info, by the SIM's operator code; a custom APN by hand. Roaming: off by default, with what it may cost. Preferred network type (5G, 4G, 3G) where the modem lets it be chosen. Airplane mode in the taskbar's quick settings: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and the modem off together (rfkill and ModemManager), and back as they were.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 3. The connection
docs.t: Connect and disconnect from the taskbar; connect automatically (on by default for the SIM's home network). Priority: cable, then Wi-Fi, then cellular; cellular stays connected but unused while Wi-Fi works, and carries the traffic within seconds when Wi-Fi drops (the routes' metrics), with a notification. The firewall applies to the cellular interface as to every other. IPv6 and IPv4 as the operator gives them (many operators are IPv6-only with NAT64/464XLAT: clat where needed).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 4. Data and money
docs.t: Metered by default on cellular (1.5.8's metered connections). Data used this month on each SIM, from the interface counters, kept across restarts; a monthly limit with a warning at 80 % and, if chosen, cellular data off at 100 %; the month's start day set by the person. Updates on cellular: never automatic; offered with the download size ("Download over mobile data: 42 MB").

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 5. Signal and status
docs.t: The taskbar shows signal bars, the network type (5G, LTE, 3G) and the operator, from ModemManager; Settings shows the signal's details (RSRP, RSRQ, SINR) for placing the computer or an antenna. System health: modem events (SIM removed, PIN blocked, no network, the module restarted). The self-test: the modem found, its driver, the SIM, registration, a data connection.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 6. Messages (SMS)
docs.t: A Messages app: conversations, read and send, delivery reports, notifications for new messages (also with the desktop locked: the sender and "new message", not the text, unless the person allows it). Messages kept in the account's folder (.rudolf/messages), and in the encrypted folder when "Encrypt my data" is on. Long messages and Unicode (multi-part SMS); MMS is left out (it needs the operator's MMS gateway and a separate APN).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 7. ARM64 (from 1.5.9's build)
docs.t: The first published ARM64 release: its own update list (beta/arm64/, stable/arm64/), a disc image for UEFI ARM64 computers, and the same parts 1 to 6. Proven in QEMU aarch64 and on one ARM64 computer before it is published.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Asked for: printing to printers plugged in by USB, as Rudolf OS prints to network printers now (rudolf-print: IPP Everywhere and AirPrint, no CUPS and no drivers). The same print dialog (WordPro, SpreadsheetPro, PresentPro, and the PDF Viewer since 1.5.9) lists them as "USB: name".

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.1 Which USB printers
docs.t: IPP over USB (the USB printer class's protocol 4, 7/1/4; most printers sold since about 2015, and every one with the IPP Everywhere or Mopria logo): the printer speaks IPP over its USB link exactly as over the network. ipp-usb (Debian's, GPL-2) turns it into a local IPP address; rudolf-print then prints to it as to a network printer (PDF, or PWG / Apple raster from pdf.js). Nothing new to write for the job itself. Plain USB printers that read PDF or PostScript (7/1/1 or 7/1/2, the IEEE 1284 device ID listing PDF or POSTSCRIPT in its command set): the job is written to /dev/usb/lpN as it is. Through the kernel's usblp driver.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.1 Which USB printers
docs.t: Others (PCL-only or host-based printers that need a driver): not in 1.5.9. The dialog names the printer and says it needs a driver Rudolf OS does not have; PCL raster from pdf.js (as PWG raster is made now) is a candidate for later.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.2 What changes
docs.t: Kernel: USB_PRINTER (usblp) as a module, checked in kconfig.sh (x86 and ARM64). usblp must not claim an IPP over USB printer's interface 7/1/4 (ipp-usb needs it): the modem service's way (mdev with the interface's class) unbinds it for those. The system layer: ipp-usb and its libraries, with a budget checked in ci_release.sh (about 10 MB expected; the build says the real size, as for ModemManager). Avahi is not added: ipp-usb's address is passed to rudolf-print in /run/rudolf/usb-printers instead of being announced on the network.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.2 What changes
docs.t: /usr/lib/rudolf/usbprint (mdev hotplug, like the modem service): a printer plugged in starts ipp-usb for it (IPP over USB) or records its /dev/usb/lpN and device ID (plain); unplugged, it stops it and forgets it. rudolfd's print/find adds these to the network's printers; print/job sends to /dev/usb/lpN for the plain kind. Settings › Devices lists a USB printer with its kind (IPP over USB, PDF, PostScript, or "needs a driver"). The self-test: a "usb-printer" line (found, its kind, ipp-usb answering).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 8. USB printers (moved from 1.5.9 on 2026-11-13) › 8.3 Tests
docs.t: Host: the hotplug script with stand-ins (an IPP over USB printer's interfaces, a plain PostScript one, a PCL-only one); rudolfd's print/find listing them; a job to the plain kind written to a stand-in /dev/usb/lp0. rudolf-print against ipp-usb's stand-in (its test IPP server) as for network printers. On real hardware: the HP desktop's user's USB printer (on the HP desktop, or on the Vivobook if it can be borrowed), first read only (its interfaces and device ID: which kind it is), then a test page.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Why: mdev makes device nodes and runs scripts, but keeps no device database and tells no program about devices. Linux software finds hardware through udev (libudev): ModemManager (1.5.9 needed a workaround: #280), libinput, SDL and Steam's controllers, PipeWire, Waydroid and many Flatpak apps. Each gap became a workaround of its own; 1.6.0's modems and the plans after it (Waydroid, PipeWire, a native or Wayland desktop) lean on udev more. Which udev: systemd-udevd on its own (from Debian's udev package; no systemd as init) or eudev, whichever is smaller and keeps working in the build; measured against a budget in ci_release.sh. The hardware database (hwdb.bin) and the packages' rules (ModemManager's, libinput's, the uaccess/joystick ones) come with it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Rudolf OS's own rules: what /etc/mdev.conf does today (the modem service, devplug's USB and phone events, joystick permissions, drives, cameras, the netplug and thunderbolt scripts) becomes rules in /usr/lib/udev/rules.d/90-rudolf.rules calling the same scripts (their ACTION/MDEV environment mapped to udev's), so the scripts change little. Start-up: rudolf-init starts udevd early, triggers coldplug and waits for it to settle (with a time limit) before the display and the services start. Recovery mode keeps mdev as a fallback: if udevd does not start, mdev does, and System health says so. What it lets go of: the modem service's --test-no-udev and its port reporting (ModemManager finds its ports itself again), devplug's own guesses where udev's tags say what a device is.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Tests: host tests of the rules with udevadm test on stand-in devices; QEMU (start-up time with udev against mdev, self-test lists, the camera, Bluetooth, sound, a controller in Steam plugged in while it runs. Done (2026-11-15), in code; measured and checked on the Vivobook at its first beta (asked for: "Implement the transition to udev as we previously planned, and just plan checks and manual tests to ensure everything still works properly"; no memory budget, as said):

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Which udev: systemd-udevd on its own and udevadm, from Ubuntu 24.04's udev package (the base layer's libraries come from it): its helpers (ata_id, cdrom_id, scsi_id, v4l_id, …), its rules, and the hardware database (hwdb.bin, built from its hwdb.d in ci_release.sh), with the libraries the base layer lacks (libsystemd-shared's at its own path). Left out: 71-seat and 73-seat-late (systemd-logind's), 90-vconsole and 99-systemd (systemd's), and 80-net-setup-link (it would rename network interfaces; Rudolf OS's scripts know eth0, wlan0 and the adapters by the kernel's names). The groups its rules name (disk, lp, kmem, dialout, cdrom, tape, render, kvm, sgx) are in /etc/group (ci_release.sh for an existing base layer, mkrootfs.sh for a new one).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Rudolf OS's own rules: /usr/lib/udev/rules.d/90-rudolf.rules, every line of /etc/mdev.conf that set an owner or ran a script: the same owners and modes (as numbers), the same scripts (sound, joyperm, rudolf-debian devices, modem, devplug, thunderbolt, netplug) through /usr/lib/rudolf/udev-run, which gives them mdev's MDEV (the name under /dev, or the interface) beside udev's ACTION, SUBSYSTEM, DEVTYPE, DEVPATH, and starts them in a session of their own so a slow one (mounting a drive, starting ModemManager) never holds up udev. Drivers are loaded by udev's 80-drivers.rules (mdev's modprobe line). The scripts themselves did not change.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Start-up: rudolf-init starts udevd (--daemon --resolve-names=early), checks it answers, announces the devices already there (subsystems, then devices) and waits for them, 15 s at most. If udevd does not start or answer, if udev is not in the build, or with rudolf.udev=0 on the start-up line, mdev does as before. /run/rudolf/devices says which ("udev", or "mdev (why)"); the self-test's new devices line fails on the fallback (skipped when asked for), and when udevd stopped or its database is empty.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: What it let go of: the modem service starts ModemManager with udev as on other Linux (no --test-no-udev, no reports of each port: it finds them through udev itself); with mdev, as in 1.5.9. Debian gets udev's database (/run/udev, read only), so Steam and SDL find controllers as on other Linux; Flatpak binds it into its sandboxes itself. devplug's own guesses were left as they are. Tests: qt/host/udev60_t.sh (13 here: rudolf-init's own lines with stand-ins, its four ways to mdev, udev-run, every mdev.conf script in a rule, the modem service, the self-test's line; with udevadm in CI also udevadm verify and udevadm test on the runner's devices), .github/workflows/udev-check.yml.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: 1. Start-up: /run/rudolf/devices says udev; the self-test's devices line passes; /run/rudolf/udev.log has no errors; start-up to the desktop no slower than 1.5.9's (System health › Last starts: 39 s on 2026111503). 2. Every device the self-test lists: its lines all as on 1.5.9 (sound, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, the camera, the GPU, storage, the listeners); ls -l /dev/input /dev/dri /dev/snd /dev/video* /dev/hidraw*: the owners and modes as under mdev (input root 0640, controllers 1000, dri 0666, snd audio 0660, cameras 1000). 3. Network: the interfaces keep their names (wlan0, eth0, usb0); Wi-Fi connects; the MiFi over USB gets an address (netplug) and shows in Network Settings; unplugged, it goes.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: 4. Sound: speakers and microphone; headphones in the jack and out; a USB or Bluetooth headset comes and goes (sound hotplug). 5. A USB stick plugged in, mounted and shown in the File Explorer, safely removed; an SD card if the computer has a reader; another Rudolf OS stick (read only, 1.5.9's 14.4). 6. The camera in Settings and in Meet (owner); in a Linux app (Debian or Flatpak). 7. A game controller plugged in later: in Rudolf's games, and in Steam while it runs (owner); Steam Input. 8. Keyboard, touchpad, a USB mouse plugged in later; the brightness and volume keys (rudolf-display).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 9. udev instead of mdev (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: 9. The modem (the USB stick when there is one): ModemManager started with udev, mmcli -L lists it, the self-test's modem line passes; unplugged, it stops. 10. Thunderbolt or USB4 if the computer has it (the test laptop): a device approved or asked about. 11. Sleep and wake (the lid): devices back, Wi-Fi reconnects. 12. The fallback: one start with rudolf.udev=0 (Developer mode's start-up options, or the boot menu's e): mdev, everything above still works as on 1.5.9, the self-test's devices line skipped. 13. Memory at idle on the Vivobook, read once with and once without (rudolf.udev=0), for the record only.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 10. A Linux user for each account (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Moved into 1.5.9 on 2026-11-14 (docs/plan-1.5.9.md Part 15.3), as part of its security work. Why: every Rudolf OS account runs as the same Linux user (rudolf, uid 1000). The desktop keeps the accounts apart, but Linux apps, Wine and Debian run as that one user and can read every account's files (the vault's own note says so). Conventional distributions give each person a Linux user of their own.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 10. A Linux user for each account (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Users: each account gets its own Linux user (uid 1001 and up), made when the account is made, removed when it is removed; its home folder (/home/NAME, still encrypted with the account's key) owned by it and readable by nobody else. The rudolf user stays for the desktop engine itself (the page and rudolfd's helpers). What runs as whom: at sign-in, rudolfd starts the account's session pieces as its user: Flatpak apps, Debian and Wine, the session D-Bus, PulseAudio (or PipeWire later), the portal; signing out stops them. Two accounts signed in one after the other never share a running app.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 10. A Linux user for each account (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Shared things: Downloads and the files the desktop page keeps per account move into each user's home; groups for the devices people use (video, audio, input for controllers, the ADB phone) replace today's chmod to uid 1000. Moving existing computers: the first start of 1.6.0 gives each existing account its user and moves its files (ownership only, no copying), checked and logged; anything that cannot move stays readable to its account and is named in System health. Tests: two accounts on the host and in QEMU: one cannot read the other's files from a Flatpak app, a Debian terminal or Wine; signing out stops the account's apps; the move on an existing data partition.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 11. Sessions and admin prompts for Linux apps: elogind and polkit (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Why: Linux apps ask login1 (systemd-logind) whether to keep the computer awake (a game, a video, a download), who is signed in and which devices the person may use; and they ask polkit for an administrator's password before doing something to the system. Rudolf OS has neither, so these requests fail or are ignored. elogind (logind without systemd): one seat, the signed-in account's session (with Part 10, its own user); apps' inhibitors (sleep, idle, lid) are honoured by Rudolf OS's own power code, which already holds off sleep for video, calls and games; rudolfd reads them through elogind instead of guessing.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 11. Sessions and admin prompts for Linux apps: elogind and polkit (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: polkit, with an agent drawn by the desktop: an app's request for an administrator shows the desktop's own password prompt (the one Settings uses), and only administrators' passwords are accepted. Rules kept short and read-only in the system layer. Budget: both together under 5 MB in the system layer, checked in ci_release.sh. docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: Asked for: a way to add system parts (a driver, firmware, a tool, a printer filter) to one computer without a new release, instead of a conventional package manager. Decided (2026-11-14): not a package manager that changes the base (apt or pacman style: every computer would end up different, updates could fail half-way, the base's signature would no longer cover what runs, and rollback would stop being clean), but signed system extensions: read-only layers over the unchanged base, as systemd's sysext and Fedora's image-based editions do. The base stays one signed image, the same on every computer, with its a/b spare and recovery.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.1 What an extension is
docs.t: An rpk package of a new kind, sysext (iso/sys/rpk.c: the same file format, download, signature check, revocation and rpk install/remove), holding files for the system: usr/bin, usr/lib (programs and libraries), lib/firmware, lib/modules/KVER/extra (kernel modules), usr/lib/udev/rules.d (after Part 9), usr/lib/cups or usr/lib/rudolf/print filters (Part 8), and at most one start script, usr/lib/rudolf/ext.d/NAME.start. builds them). A Library or developer key can never sign one (rpk refuses, as it refuses Library programs today).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.1 What an extension is
docs.t: Tied to the base it was built for: PKGINFO base = ABI (a hash of the base layer's libraries, written into the base as usr/share/rudolf/base-abi by ci_release.sh) and, for kernel modules, kernel = KVER. Kernel modules are built in the same run as the kernel, so they carry its module signature.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.2 How it is put in place
docs.t: At each start, before the desktop (the initramfs, or early in init): every installed, enabled extension that matches this base's ABI (and kernel) is mounted read-only at /run/rudolf/ext/NAME, and the system's /usr, /lib/firmware and /lib/modules/KVER/extra become read-only overlays (overlayfs, lower layers only: the extensions over the base, in a fixed order by name). Nothing is ever written into the base. A file the base already has may not be replaced (checked while assembling): an extension adds, it does not override, so one cannot change what the signed base does. A clash leaves that extension out, named in System health.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 13. Signed system extensions (added on 2026-11-14) › 13.3 Safety
docs.t: A bad extension cannot stop Rudolf starting: the first start after installing one is a trial (as Native's): if the desktop does not come up, the next start leaves out the extensions installed since the last good start and says so. The start menu's recovery entry and Recovery mode always start without extensions. Updates: before switching slots, rudolf-update fetches each installed extension's build for the new base (the extensions' repository has one per base ABI). One that has no build for it yet is kept but left out after the update, with a notice and System health's line, and comes back when its build appears. An update never fails because of an extension.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: Found on the Vivobook (2026-11-14): signing in to the Claude app for Linux with an e-mail address showed a notice that GNOME Keyring is not set up. Linux apps (the Claude app, VS Code, Chromium-based and Electron apps, mail and chat apps) keep their sign-ins and tokens through the Secret Service (org.freedesktop.secrets, libsecret). Rudolf OS has none, so they warn, keep the secret in a plain file (Electron's basic text store) or forget it and ask again after every restart.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: The service: gnome-keyring-daemon's secrets component only (no SSH or GPG agent, no GUI of its own), in Debian's container and for Flatpak apps (the portal's Secret interface), started with the account's session pieces (1.5.9's Part 15.3: each account its own Linux user, so each account its own keyring, in its own encrypted home). Unlocked by the sign-in: the keyring's password is the account's own; the sign-in (and the lock screen) hand it to the daemon (as pam_gnome_keyring does) so no second password is asked; changing the account's password changes the keyring's; signing out locks it. An account without a password gets a keyring kept with the account's encryption key instead of a password.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: The service: /usr/lib/rudolf/keyring, started by rudolfd at sign-in (au_session_start, after the session bus and the portal) as the account's Linux user with its session's environment: gnome-keyring-daemon `--foreground --components=secrets` (no SSH or GPG agent, no window), on the account's session bus, which Debian's programs (its /run/user/1000/bus) and Flatpak apps with --talk-name=org.freedesktop.secrets reach. Signing out stops it with the account's other programs. Its log: /run/rudolf/keyring-UID.log; its socket ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/keyring/) is in the list of listeners.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: Unlocked by the sign-in, without the password: decided instead of handing the password to the daemon. The keyring is the account's "login" keyring in its own folder (~/.local/share/keyrings), made the first time as a keyring with no password of its own (gnome-keyring's text format) and the default. The folder is encrypted with the account's key, is only its user's (0700, the files 0600), and is there only while the account is signed in: so no second password is asked, a password change needs nothing, sign-out shuts it away, and removing the account removes it. A keyring already there (one made in Debian with a password, say) is never changed.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)

The desktop's own processes keep "Rudolf". Budget: gnome-keyring-daemon and the libraries the base layer lacks, 3 MB, checked in ci_release.sh (the release workflow installs gnome-keyring on the build machine).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: The Secret portal for Flatpak apps (rudolf-portal, org.freedesktop.portal.Secret version 1): libsecret inside a Flatpak sandbox keeps the app's secrets in a file of its own (~/.var/app/ID/data/keyrings), encrypted with a secret the portal gives it through RetrieveSecret(fd). That secret is the app's own (64 random bytes), made once and kept in the account's folder (~/.local/share/rudolf/app-secrets/ID, 0700/0600): so it is as safe as the keyring, the same each time, another app's different. A program outside a sandbox is refused (it uses the Secret Service).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 14. A keyring for Linux apps: the Secret Service (added on 2026-11-14)
docs.t: rudolf-portal is gcr's prompter (org.gnome.keyring.SystemPrompter on the account's session bus, which gnome-keyring-daemon asks; gcr-prompter, a GNOME window, is not in Rudolf OS): gcr's protocol as gcr-system-prompter.c speaks it (org.gnome.keyring.internal.Prompter's BeginPrompting, PerformPrompt and StopPrompting; the daemon's org.gnome.keyring.internal.Prompter.Callback PromptReady and PromptDone; one prompt at a time, the others waiting; the properties sent back as gcr sends them, a new password's strength among them, so the daemon asks "Store passwords unencrypted?" only for an empty one), and its secret exchange "[sx-aes-1]" as gcr-secret-exchange.c does it (Diffie-Hellman in IKE's 1536-bit group, HKDF-SHA256 to a 16-byte key, AES-128-CBC with PKCS#7 padding, its key-file messages), with OpenSSL's libcrypto, which the base layer already has (no new library; the portal is built with -lcrypto in mkrootfs.sh, ci_release.sh and the ARM64 check). Weak public keys (1, p-1, p) are refused.
